name: Korean eyebrow shaping (willow leaf / crescent)

card.summary: Traditional Korean eyebrow shapes, the willow-leaf and crescent brows of Joseon-era beauty writing, which people reference when shaping softer, gently curved brows that frame the eyes.
card.note: Brow shaping by waxing, threading or tinting can irritate skin; permanent makeup carries its own risks.

quick.overview:
Korean eyebrow shaping in the historical sense refers to named brow shapes, such as the willow-leaf and crescent, recorded in Joseon-era writing on women's beauty. The shapes are soft and gently curved, and they are used as a reference for brows that frame the eyes without a sharp arch.

The appearance payoff is a softer, balanced upper face. Brows are among the most changeable features, since they can be shaped, filled or tinted, which is why historical shapes are a popular source of ideas.
quick.how: In practice people use brow pencil, powder, tinting, trimming or professional shaping to approximate a rounded crescent or a leaf-like curve that is thickest near the middle and tapers at the tail. Some choose semi-permanent brow makeup to keep a consistent shape.
quick.risks: Plucking and waxing can cause redness or irritation, over-removal can leave gaps that regrow slowly, and tattooing or microblading carries infection, pigment and dissatisfaction risks.

lead: Korean eyebrow shaping, in the historical sense, refers to the named brow shapes found in accounts of Korean women's beauty, notably the willow-leaf and crescent brows. A Korea JoongAng Daily report says an 1809 women's text, Gyuhapchongsuh, identifies ten different eyebrow curves, and curator Lee Ji-sun is quoted calling this evidence of the "aesthetic importance of the eyebrow" [1]. A second feature in the same paper reports that researchers studying late Joseon paintings of beautiful women identified crescent-shaped eyebrows as a common trait [2].

People interested in these shapes use them as a model for soft, curved brows: a rounded crescent, or a leaf-like shape that tapers at the end. A beauty blog summarising Joseon-era writing says books on women's habits list about ten designs with names such as willow and crescent [3].

chain: Choose a soft crescent or willow-leaf shape
Shape, fill or tint brows to follow it
Gentler framing of the eyes and a softer upper face
angle.text: Brow shape changes how the eyes and upper face read. A gently curved crescent or tapered leaf-shaped brow is a drawn, filled or trimmed shape that people use for a softer look than a sharp arch.

paras: Joseon (1392 to 1910) writing on women's habits records about ten brow designs, with names such as willow and crescent, according to a beauty blog summarising the period [3]. The 1809 Gyuhapchongsuh is described as a major reference text for Joseon women and as identifying ten brow curves, with shapes rarely uniform [1].

Researchers at Kyungpook National University, as reported by the Korea JoongAng Daily, linked crescent brows in late Joseon portraits to a "soft, wise, economical and brilliant" disposition prized in women at the time [2]. The BeautyTap piece also notes that gisaeng entertainers popularised inked brows, while noble yangban women avoided heavy makeup [3].

timeline.event: Joseon period, in which writing on women's beauty records about ten named brow designs [3].
